Human factors analysis can be used to advance our understanding of the true nature of errors in complex work settings. Research in this area has identified factors that contribute to inefficiencies and quantified the effects of human and organizational factors on performance of critical tasks. The forensic science community can benefit from the application of the substantial body of human factors work to reduce the likelihood and consequences of human error in the scientific interpretation of evidence. To assist the forensic community in this effort, the National Institute of Justice (NIJ) and the National Institute of Standards and Technology’s Special Programs Office partnered to develop a series of expert panels to examine human factors in forensic analyses and develop practices to reduce the likelihood of error based on scientific research. pages.text: Human jaws are surprisingly strong and efficient | National Geographic SCIENCE NOT EXACTLY ROCKET SCIENCE Human jaws are surprisingly strong and efficient By Ed Yong Published June 22, 2010 • 4 min read Stephen Wroe has built a career out of analysing some of the planet’s most formidable skulls. His group at the University of New South Wales have studied the strength, sturdiness and biting power of the sabre-toothed cat , the great white shark , and the Komodo dragon . Now, he has turned his attention to a predator whose skull is far less impressive but yields surprises all the same – us. Humans, it is said, have relatively weak jaws that can’t inflict or withstand high bite forces. Some have suggested that we are adapted to eat foods that aren’t very tough, or that our use of tools and cooking has lessened the evolutionary pressure on maintaining sturdy jaws. Some have even suggested that our weedy jaw muscles made way for our large brains and thus facilitated their evolution. But according to Wroe, all of these explanations have a fatal flaw – our jaws aren’t weak at all. They’re actually remarkably efficient for a primate. The notion of weak human chops was based on very unrefined models that treated our jaws as two-dimensional levers. Of course, in real life, we chew in three glorious dimensions. To really understand how strong our mandibles are, we need to add that third dimension to the models. That’s exactly what Wroe did. He used his signature technique, called finite element analysis , to create a virtual model of a human skull (belonging to a San hunter-gatherer).

Get the Facts A new study has dropped a bombshell on archaeology, claiming signs of human activity in the Americas far earlier than thought. By Michael Greshko Published April 26, 2017 • 15 min read In an announcement sure to spark a firestorm of controversy, researchers say they’ve found signs of ancient humans in California between 120,000 and 140,000 years ago—more than a hundred thousand years before humans were thought to exist anywhere in the Americas. pages.text: Humans used to have straighter teeth—what changed? | National Geographic HEALTH Humans used to have straighter teeth—what changed? New research explores how diet, evolution, and facial anatomy may have shaped our modern smiles. Studies of ancient skulls show wider jaws and fewer malocclusions, leading researchers to explore how diet and lifestyle shaped the human face. Photograph by Alan/Adobe Stock By Leah Worthington Published July 15, 2025 Braces, rubber bands, even jaw surgery—millions endure them in pursuit of a straighter smile. But were misaligned smiles always this common? Research suggests that might not be the case. While malocclusions—crowded or misaligned teeth—have been found among our hunter-gatherer ancestors, they appear to be more prevalent in modern populations. So what changed? Experts say the answer isn’t simple but point to one possible culprit: our diets. As we traded raw, tough foods for softer, more processed ones, the burden of chewing decreased, allowing our jaws to shrink over time. Now, researchers are exploring how evolutionary biology, diet, and modern lifestyles may have reshaped our faces—and our smiles. How farming may have reshaped the human face Ancient human skulls were strikingly different from our own. Early hunter-gatherers had large, powerful jaws built for the demanding work of chewing tough meats, fibrous vegetables, seeds, and nuts. But around 12,000 years ago, things began to change. pages.text: Hundreds still homeless after 'unsafe' Canning Town flats evacuation Skip to content Site search Home News Sport Business Technology Health Culture Arts Travel Earth Audio Video Live Documentaries Weather Newsletters Watch Live Hundreds still homeless after being evacuated from 'unsafe' flats 4 hours ago Share Save Add as preferred on Google Ayshea Buksh London BBC The Royal Gateway, also known as Caxton Works, was advertised as "an exciting regeneration project" when it was built Hundreds of residents in east London remain homeless after structural defects were discovered at an award-winning high-rise development that was declared "at risk of sudden collapse". The Royal Gateway, also known as Caxton Works in Canning Town, Newham, was built less than 10 years ago. But last month, people living there were suddenly told to leave - some in the middle of the night by London Fire Brigade - because it was "unsafe". Businesses renting commercial spaces were also told to evacuate their premises. Engineers identified concerns with reinforced concrete "transfer slabs" supporting the buildings - an issue that has emerged at other London developments, prompting wider scrutiny of the construction method. Property company Galliard Homes, which built the scheme, says it is working to "investigate the concerns and develop potential solutions", while giving financial and practical support to residents. pages.text: Hungary v Northern Ireland: We want to play on the biggest stages - Isaac Price - BBC Sport Image source, Press Eye Image caption, West Brom midfielder Isaac Price has started Northern Ireland's last 25 matches By Andy Gray BBC Sport NI Journalist Published 16 November 2026 When Northern Ireland step out into the Puskas Arena on Tuesday night, they hope it will be a taste of what is to come. In the 70,000-seater stadium, which hosted the Champions League final between Paris St-Germain and Arsenal in May, Northern Ireland's destiny will be in their own hands. In 18 months' time, Michael O'Neill's young side will hope be at the Euro 2028 finals. But for now, they face Hungary with hopes of promotion to League A in the Nations League for the first time. A win or a draw will do the job in Budapest, and it would be the latest step for a Northern Ireland side who continue to show encouraging signs in their development. Worst case, NI will still have a shot at a play-off for League A in March but their sole aim is to get the job done on Tuesday. Midfielder Isaac Price, who has grown into a key player under O'Neill, says you "have got to love the expectation". "That's what you play football for. We're playing in a stadium where 70,000 people will be watching and then there'll be loads more at home watching," he told BBC Sport NI. "That's what you grow up and want to do. You've got to play on the biggest stages and that's what it'll be tomorrow [Tuesday] night." Hunting Hunting Image Details Hunting is available at more than 400 units of the National Wildlife Refuge System (national wildlife refuges and wetland management districts) and almost 20 national fish hatcheries. Hunting can be a habitat management tool to keep wildlife populations in check. Hunters' purchase of Duck Stamps helps buy conservation lands and is one of several ways hunters support conservation. All hunters must possess valid state hunting licenses. Be sure to also check regulations for each state and FWS location when planning your hunt. Related Stories Why Hunting Is Allowed on Refuges Hunting is deeply rooted in America’s heritage, and it can be an important wildlife management tool. Several laws and U.S. Fish and Wildlife Service policy permit hunting on a national wildlife refuge when it is compatible with the purposes for which the refuge was established and acquired. Hydraulic Properties The Office of Geothermal’s Innovative Methods to Control Hydraulic Properties of Enhanced Geothermal Systems (EGS) , or Hydraulic Properties, initiative supports the research, development, demonstration, and deployment of technologies and techniques to control the fluid flow within the fracture network in EGS reservoirs in order to optimize them for heat extraction. EGS systems use human-made reservoirs to access subsurface heat where natural subsurface conditions lack sufficient fluid flow—or permeability—or water to allow heat to be drawn to the surface for energy. Projects under this initiative are developing targeted and reversible in-reservoir fracture permeability modification systems or methods and yield long-term reservoir productivity improvements. The ability to customize reservoirs via these methods will increase reservoir efficiency and longevity, ultimately helping to drive down EGS costs, reduce the risk of development, and accelerate the path towards widespread commercialization. Hydrothermal Resources What Are Hydrothermal Resources? The natural formation of a hydrothermal resource requires three principal elements: heat, water, and permeability. When water is heated in the earth, hot water or steam is trapped in porous and fractured rocks beneath a layer of relatively impermeable caprock, resulting in the formation of a hydrothermal reservoir. If the conditions underground are right, humans can harness that geothermal hot water or steam by drilling and then bring it to the surface to generate electricity . These types of geothermal systems typically occur close to tectonic plate boundaries, like in the western portions of the United States. Sometimes the resource is easy to find because of indicators on the surface like hot springs. Other times, conventional geothermal resources are “ hidden ,” with no signs of the underground reservoir on the surface. Hydrothermal resources are considered conventional geothermal resources because they can be developed using existing technologies and do not require creation of human-made reservoirs as needed with enhanced geothermal systems . Purpose The HMP is designed to help health care organizations: Improve the quality of care for the patients they serve. Reduce the number of patients with uncontrolled hypertension. Improve patients' overall health and well-being. The HMP is effective in promoting hypertension control among patients in health care settings that serve populations at higher risk of hypertension. This includes patients without health insurance. CDC's Division for Heart Disease and Stroke Prevention (DHDSP) developed the HMP Toolkit to provide health care organizations with the information and resources they need to implement the HMP and improve hypertension control among their patients. pages.text: I felt nothing but numbness at my dad’s death – but then I read the book he gave me on my wedding day | Culture | The Guardian Skip to main content Skip to navigation Illustration: Martin O'Neill/The Guardian View image in fullscreen Illustration: Martin O'Neill/The Guardian My cultural awakening Culture I felt nothing but numbness at my dad’s death – but then I read the book he gave me on my wedding day Dylan Thomas’s Under Milk Wood reminded me of my dad’s decency and mischief. I laughed as I cried, and realised there’s no right way to go through the grieving process Ioan Marc Jones Sat 14 Nov 2026 07.00 EST Last modified on Sat 14 Nov 2026 10.39 EST Share Prefer the Guardian on Google I expected to break. But I felt nothing. I did not cry, nor struggle to sleep. I seldom thought of him. I felt only guilt about how little I felt. Ours was a complex relationship. As a teen, I often resented my dad, occasionally despised him. I expected the world and found disappointment. But, as I grew older, I understood that he had struggles of his own. I learned to appreciate his decency and humour, his ability to make everyone laugh with only a few words. I loved my dad, from the first time he held me to the last time I held him. But still, as weeks turned into months, I struggled to grieve. Then, when my partner and I rearranged our bookshelves, I found the first edition of Under Milk Wood that my parents gave us on our wedding day. I turned the cover and saw the note: “And all the bells of the tills of the town shall ring for our wedding.” It was my mum’s writing, but my dad’s idea.

Cancer treatment and your blood sugar Chemotherapy , or chemo, helps kill or shrink cancer cells, but it also hurts some healthy cells. This can cause side effects, like mouth sores, nausea, vomiting, and loss of appetite. These side effects may make it hard to eat, which could cause low blood sugar. Radiation therapy kills cancer cells by using high-energy rays. Radiation therapy causes your body to release extra sugar to help cope with the treatment. "There's a pivotal scene in a prison yard, and we're singing Silent Night with the Ghost of Christmas Present and Johnny Depp there," recalls Bedfordshire's Colin Fraser. Depp plays the title character Ebenezer Scrooge in the Charles Dickens tale, starring alongside Rupert Grint, Sir Ian McKellen and Daisy Ridley. Fraser, 55, who has appeared in West End shows such as The Lion King, landed his current role when London Voices, his choir, was asked to audition for the film. He says that despite the spooky setting, the renditions of Silent Night and other carols are "completely straight" and "very traditional". "We sang them traditionally in four-part harmony as we would every year," he says. "There's a street scene and we're around the Christmas tree, singing – I think it was I Saw Three Ships Come Sailing In. "There was all the snow being pumped in and it felt like a very traditional Christmas." Jaap Buitendi

pages.description: The cricket boards of Scotland and the Netherlands criticise the International Cricket Council for structural changes made to men's 50-over World Cup.
pages.text: ICC criticised for 'disrespectful' changes to World Cup by Cricket Scotland and KNCB - BBC Sport Image source, Getty Images Image caption, Richie Berrington and Bas de Leede are the current captains of Scotland and the Netherlands respectively By Timothy Abraham BBC Sport Journalist Published 10 August 2026 The cricket boards of Scotland and the Netherlands have criticised the International Cricket Council for structural changes made to the men's 50-over World Cup. Last month the ICC announced the main part of the tournament for 2027 would be 12 teams in two groups of six, rather than 14 as originally planned. The three lowest-ranked qualifiers will instead be placed in a preliminary three-team Super Series, from which only the winner will progress. It effectively means the likes of Scotland and the Netherlands could face three qualifying tournaments to reach the main group stage of the World Cup. A joint statement from Cricket Scotland and Royal Dutch Cricket Association (KNCB) said they had "significant concerns" about the "impact of these changes" along with the "process through which they have been introduced". "The changes risk weakening the integrity and credibility of international cricket, and only highlights the importance of strong governance, transparent decision-making and effective engagement with members," the statement said. "Changing those structures at short notice creates significant uncertainty, disrupts planning, and places additional operational and financial pressure on organisations that are already operating with limited resources." pages.text: ICE agents pepper spray pregnant US citizen in California, video shows | ICE (US Immigration and Customs Enforcement) | The Guardian Skip to main content Skip to navigation 0:46 Pregnant woman pepper sprayed and thrown to ground by ICE agents in California – video ICE (US Immigration and Customs Enforcement) ICE agents pepper spray pregnant US citizen in California, video shows Lizbeth Vargas Andrade, 23, was arrested after being pushed to the ground and on to her stomach, her attorney says Sam Levin Tue 17 Nov 2026 17.24 EST First published on Mon 16 Nov 2026 13.48 EST Share Prefer the Guardian on Google US Immigration and Customs Enforcement (ICE) agents pepper-sprayed a pregnant US citizen and threw her to the ground during a protest in California on Sunday, according to her family’s attorney, who shared footage of the incident. Lizbeth Vargas Andrade, 23, was filming and protesting against the presence of several ICE officers outside the Stanislaus county jail in Modesto, in California’s Central valley, before she was taken down by officers and arrested while she was lying on her stomach during a chaotic encounter. Vargas Andrade, who is 12 weeks pregnant, said in a press conference on Sunday evening that she was part of a group of local residents who monitor ICE sightings, and that she had gone to the jail parking lot after agents were spotted in the area. A commotion erupted when ICE agents moved to arrest a man who, it appeared, had just been released from the jail, video shows. NPS Winter conditions often last over six months in parts of Alaska. Ice and snow dominate the landscape, greatly influencing the natural world. Plants and animals have adapted to this frozen world, and so have the humans who depend on these resources. Glaciers and sea ice are two of the most well-known ice features affected by climate change's warmer temperatures. As the ice changes, so do people’s lifestyles and ways of thinking about the places they live. In Skagway, ice appears as high mountain glaciers, and frozen lakes and rivers. In Nome, sea ice is critical to continuing traditions of harvesting subsistence foods. Melting Glaciers When you ask about changing ice conditions in Skagway, talk immediately turns to glaciers. There are glaciers in the mountains above White Pass, the Chilkoot Trail, and across Taiya Inlet and Lynn Canal. Like many places around the world, warming temperatures are having a serious effect on the glaciers near Skagway. The images were so powerful, one ended up on the cover. Mark Thiessen Story and photographs by Mattias Klum Published May 11, 2026 This story originally published in the June 2001 issue of National Geographic magazine. See more digitized stories from our archives here . Can India’s last lions be saved? In the latest issue of National Geographic, we revisit the world’s only existing population of Asiatic lions 20 years later as they overrun a small reserve in western India. Read our June 2026 story Most people think of lions as strictly African beasts, but only because they've been killed off almost everywhere else. Ten thousand years ago lions spanned vast sections of the globe, and so did people, who—as they multiplied and organized—put pressure on competitors at the top of the food chain. Now lions hold only a small fraction of their former habitat, and Asiatic lions, a subspecies that split from African lions perhaps 100,000 years ago, hang on to an almost impossibly small slice of their former domain. India is the proud steward of these 300 or so lions, which live primarily in a 560-square-mile sanctuary. It took me a year and a half to get a permit to explore the entire Gir Forest—and no time at all to see why these lions became symbols of royalty and greatness. Search Twitter YouTube Facebook Instagram Flickr LinkedIn Idaho Falls District Office The Idaho Falls District, located in southeast Idaho, manages approximately 3.7 million acres of public land. The topography and terrain differ substantially throughout the area, ranging from sagebrush and desert to high-elevation forests. The District itself incorporates 16 counties, with Montana to the north and Utah to the south. The western edge borders the Craters of the Moon National Monument and Preserve, with the eastern edge extending to the beautiful Teton mountain range. With such a diverse geographic area, the Idaho Falls District has many challenges to face as it balances its mission of multiple use and sustainable yield to achieve a sustainable ecosystem. Some of the major activities occurring within the district include: grazing, recreation, mining, wildlife and fisheries, fire management, riparian and wetland management, realty and land use. The Idaho Falls District is divided into four geographic areas/field offices: Challis (799,000 acres), Salmon (493,000 acres), Upper Snake (1,854,000 acres) and Pocatello (557,000 acres). Her early work focused on resource management planning and National Environmental Policy Act work—skills she took to western Oregon for years to plan timber sales, recreation, and other management activities. Conry began her career with the BLM 21 years ago, starting as a Presidential Management Fellow in Washington, DC, after completing her master’s in forestry at the University of Montana.

Congress established the Iditarod as a National Historic Trail in 1978. It is the isolated, primitive quality of this historical environment that makes the National Historic Iditarod Trail proposal unique. Nowhere in the National Trail System is there such an extensive landscape, so demanding of durability and skill during its winter season of travel.
